clue.text: Was Tyburn part of this London ?

definitions.text: Was Tyburn part of this London ?

parts.words: Was Tyburn part of this London ?
parts.note: Tyburn was London's old gallows, where the hanged swung; the 1960s city of fashion and pop was called by the same word

explanation.surface: A history question about whether old Tyburn belonged to the lively London of the sixties.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyburn, near today's Marble Arch, was where London hanged its criminals until 1783, so it was a place of bodies swinging from ropes.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1960s capital of fashion and music was nicknamed for its lively, permissive mood, and a hanged body also sways from the rope.

clue.text: This place could give one the pip !

definitions.text: This place could give one the pip !

parts.words: This place could give one the pip !
parts.note: to give someone the pip is to annoy them, but a pip is also the star on an army officer's shoulder, earned at the military college

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a certain place gets on their nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give one the pip' is British slang for annoy; a pip is also the star on a junior army officer's uniform, which the Royal Military Academy awards its cadets.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Military Academy in Berkshire trains British army officers, who receive their first rank insignia there.

clue.text: It requires an effort to make this river work

definitions.text: It requires an effort to make this river work

parts.words: It requires an effort to make this river work
parts.note: adding the word try, an effort, to the river's name spells a word for work or diligence

explanation.surface: An engineer finds it hard going to put a river to use.
explanation.walkthrough: The Asian river's name plus TRY (an effort) makes INDUSTRY, which means work.
explanation.definitionFit: The great river of Pakistan, flowing from Tibet to the Arabian Sea, takes its name from the Sanskrit for river.

clue.text: Suitable fare for those watching the waistline ?

definitions.text: Suitable fare for those watching the waistline ?

parts.words: Suitable fare for those watching the waistline ?
parts.note: dieters watch their middles, and the griddle-baked scones of northern Britain take their name from a word for a corset or belt

explanation.surface: A question about which food suits people on a diet.
explanation.walkthrough: Girdle cakes are scones baked on a girdle, the Scots and northern English word for a griddle; a girdle is also a corset worn to slim the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat scones cooked on a griddle plate are named for the Scottish word for that pan, which is also a slimming garment.

clue.text: Cuts nothing, one might say

indicators.note: the phrase points to how the word is spoken rather than written

parts.note: nix is slang for nothing

explanation.surface: Someone claims that cuts amount to nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Small notches or shallow wounds are both cuts in the sense of slight incisions.

clue.text: Middlesex barman at the wheel

parts.note: a man from ... Bar, a town once in the county of Middlesex, whose craft is throwing clay on a turning wheel

explanation.surface: A pub barman from Middlesex is driving a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barman' reads as a pub worker, but it is a man of Potters Bar, then a Middlesex town; 'at the wheel' is not driving but the clay-shaping wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker of clay pots works at a spinning wheel, and the name also fits a resident of Potters Bar.

clue.text: Singularly wild for a youthful broadcaster

definitions.text: Singularly wild for a youthful broadcaster

parts.words: Singularly wild for a youthful broadcaster
parts.note: the young are said to sow their wild grains; the singular of that grain is what such a sower scatters

explanation.surface: A young radio presenter behaves in a remarkably reckless way.
explanation.walkthrough: To sow one's wild oats is to have a reckless youth; a broadcaster is one who scatters seed, and 'Singularly' asks for one grain, not the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A cereal grain sown by hand; the idiom of youthful excess speaks of sowing them wild.

clue.text: Part of a begging-letter from a bounder ?

definitions.text: Part of a begging-letter from a bounder ?

parts.words: Part of a begging-letter from a bounder ?
parts.note: a request for money is a touch; and a ball bouncing out crosses the side boundary of a football pitch

explanation.surface: A bit of a scrounging note written by a cad.
explanation.walkthrough: To touch someone is to ask them for money, so a line in a begging letter is a touch line. A bounder is both a cad and a bouncing ball crossing the pitch's side boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: The side boundary of a football or rugby field, beyond which the ball is out of play.

clue.text: One who mounts a proposition ?

definitions.meaning: someone who gets on a horse or bicycle
in geometry a further proposition that follows from one already proved, or a clause added to a bill

explanation.surface: Someone climbing up to make an offer.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseback travellers mount their steeds; in logic and law the same word means an added clause or corollary.

clue.text: Admirers turned and ran when pinched

indicators.note: turned tells you the word for admirers is read back to front

parts.note: fans are admirers or devotees
fled is a synonym of ran, as in ran away

explanation.surface: A group of admirers turned and ran when someone pinched them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinched' at the end looks like part of the story, but it is the definition, slang for stolen; 'turned' works only on the admirers, and 'and' and 'when' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: To grab or steal something quickly is slang for having pinched it.

clue.text: It's the lowest of the low !

definitions.text: It's the lowest of the low !

parts.words: It's the lowest of the low !
parts.note: the phrase for a despised person stands for the point directly beneath an observer, or the lowest point of anything

explanation.surface: Someone is being scorned as the most contemptible of people.
explanation.definitionFit: In astronomy and figuratively this word names the very bottom point, the opposite of the zenith.

clue.text: Study the rudest amendment when translated

parts.note: to con is an old word for to study or learn by heart

indicators.note: an amendment alters a text, so the letters of rudest are rearranged

explanation.surface: A student is told to study a rude passage once it has been changed into another language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' looks like a command but gives the old verb meaning learn by heart; 'amendment' signals the rearrangement, and 'the' and 'when' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: To construe a passage is to interpret or render it, as a translator does.

clue.text: Hastens, to confound sleuths

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into disorder, so the letters of sleuths are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone hurries off in order to baffle the detectives on their trail.
explanation.definitionFit: To hurry someone along or move with haste and energy are both senses of the verb.

clue.text: One of four brought to book

definitions.text: One of four brought to book

parts.words: One of four brought to book
parts.note: A. E. W. Mason's novel about cowardice is titled after four white plumes, so one of them appears in a book

explanation.surface: One of a group of four criminals is finally caught and punished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought to book' suggests punishment, but here it means put into a book: Mason's 1902 novel The Four Feathers, where white plumes brand a man a coward.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the four white plumes in Mason's novel is a single quill from a bird's plumage.

clue.text: A present-day recurrence

parts.note: present-day reads as modern but means a day for gifts, coming round once a year

explanation.surface: Something that keeps happening in modern times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present-day' looks like 'modern', but it means a day of giving presents, which comes round yearly.
explanation.definitionFit: A date marked each year, such as a wedding or birthday, when gifts are often exchanged.

clue.text: " With reference to your letter of ancient date .. "

definitions.text: " With reference to your letter of ancient date .. "

parts.words: " With reference to your letter of ancient date .. "
parts.note: the opening of a business letter, read as an adjective describing the characters of an old alphabet

explanation.surface: A business reply begins by referring to a letter sent long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: The office phrase 'with reference to your letter' is read literally: the adjective refers to letters, the characters of the old Germanic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the characters of the ancient Germanic alphabet, carved letters used before the Roman script.

clue.text: Worse than the Nineties ?

parts.note: the 1890s were called the Naughty Nineties, so anything worse would be more mischievous still

explanation.surface: A question whether the present is worse than the 1890s.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1890s are known as the 'Naughty Nineties' for their supposed permissiveness.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of badly behaved, describing something worse than the decade famed for its mischief.

clue.text: Game horse calls for a dance, we hear

indicators.note: the phrase says the words are to be taken by their sound, not spelling

parts.note: polo is a game played on horseback, and neighs are the calls a horse makes

explanation.surface: During a game, a horse whinnies as though asking to dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A stately Polish processional dance in triple time, also a musical form used by Chopin.

clue.text: Convulsive trouble on the line? Just as you say

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another means it is written after it

parts.note: a phone line, the telephone
a tic is an involuntary twitch or spasm

explanation.surface: A nervous twitch afflicts someone during a phone call; they agree with everything said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' in a down clue puts TIC below PHONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Phonetic spelling writes words exactly as they are pronounced.

clue.text: School fees by instalments ?

parts.note: paying bit by bit is on gentle credit; school fees are charged per term

explanation.surface: Parents ask whether school fees may be paid bit by bit.
explanation.walkthrough: Payment in instalments is buying on easy terms, and school fees are billed by the term.
explanation.definitionFit: Gentle credit conditions for paying in parts, which here also means school terms that are not hard.

clue.text: The main route to Box Hill ?

definitions.text: The main route to Box Hill ?

parts.words: The main route to Box Hill ?
parts.note: a trunk is a large box, so a route to a box is a trunk route; and the main road is the arterial highway

explanation.surface: A driver asks the best road to Box Hill, a beauty spot in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: Box Hill is a well-known hill in Surrey, England. A trunk is a box for luggage, and the main highway is the 'trunk' road.
explanation.definitionFit: A major arterial highway carrying long-distance traffic, which is just what a main route is.

clue.text: Scenes from The Merry Wives ?

indicators.note: merry suggests a tipsy jumble, so the letters of the following word are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone recalls scenes from Shakespeare's comedy The Merry Wives of Windsor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Merry Wives' looks like the Shakespeare title, but 'Merry' is the anagram signal working on WIVES; 'from The' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospects or vistas seen from a vantage point are what scenes are.

clue.text: A sorry way to tie the knot

definitions.text: A sorry way to tie the knot

parts.words: A sorry way to tie the knot
parts.note: the proverb 'marry in a hurry, repent at leisure' says such a wedding leads to regret

explanation.surface: A remark on a wedding that turns out to be regretted.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb runs 'Marry in haste, repent at leisure': a hurried wedding is the one that leaves you sorry.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb warns that a hurried marriage brings later regret, so a rushed manner is the sorry one.

clue.text: Undercover aspect of one with a note to the editor

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
an aspect is a compass direction a building faces, and N is north
B is a note of the musical scale
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An undercover agent with a note for the newspaper editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aspect' here is the way a house faces, such as N for north.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tucked under the blankets is literally beneath the covers.

clue.text: Olivine's fairy marriage portion

parts.note: a peri is a fairy or sprite of Persian legend
dot is an old word for a dowry, the portion a bride brings to a marriage

explanation.surface: A girl named Olivine has a dowry given her by a fairy godmother.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'Olivine's' stands for 'is'. Olivine sounds like a girl's name, but it is a green mineral.
explanation.definitionFit: This green gemstone is the transparent gem-quality variety of the mineral olivine.

clue.text: Judges of a plane engaged in aerobatics ?

indicators.note: a plane doing loops and rolls tumbles about, so its letters are tumbled too

explanation.surface: Judges score an aircraft performing stunts.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of assessors at a competition is a jury of experts.

clue.text: Many go both ways in concealment

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number

indicators.note: the word go is read backwards and then forwards, both directions

explanation.surface: Crowds go back and forth while hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'both ways' makes the single 'go' work twice, once backwards and once forwards, after the Roman numeral for 500; to 'lie doggo' is old slang for hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie low and keep hidden is to stay out of sight, hiding motionless.

clue.text: Builder's bakery ?

parts.note: a builder's bakery would bake bricks rather than bread, which is what a kiln for clay blocks does

explanation.surface: A question about where a builder goes for bread.
explanation.definitionFit: A furnace in which shaped clay blocks are fired hard is where building material gets baked.

clue.text: How do they know in Scotland ?

definitions.text: How do they know in Scotland ?

parts.words: How do they know in Scotland ?
parts.note: the question means 'what word do Scots use for know?', the Scots verb meaning to know

explanation.surface: A question about how people in Scotland come to learn things.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic 'do' turns the question into 'what word do they use for know?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scots verb for being aware of or acquainted with something.

clue.text: Diviner who sounds a bore

indicators.note: sounds says the word is to be taken by its pronunciation

parts.note: an auger is a tool for boring holes

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller is described as a tedious person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bore' reads as a tedious person, but it is the hole-boring tool, AUGER, pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Rome this official foretold events from the flight of birds, much as a soothsayer does.

clue.text: Bold District Attorney and his circle

parts.note: DA is the standard abbreviation for an American district attorney
a ring is a circle, or a close-knit group of associates

explanation.surface: A fearless prosecutor and his clique of associates.
explanation.definitionFit: Courageous and adventurous people show boldness in taking risks.

clue.text: Out for a good time, they take juvenile roles

definitions.text: Out for a good time, they take juvenile roles

parts.words: Out for a good time, they take juvenile roles
parts.note: pleasure-seeking men are described, and the word also splits to mean actors who play lads

explanation.surface: Fun-seeking young actors who are cast as youngsters.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer split in two is a stage instruction: actors who play boys, so take juvenile roles.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealthy pleasure-seeking men are known by this term, and split it describes actors cast as lads.
